MOSCHELLA (1961) reported malignant melanoma of the skin in sisters.
SALAMON et al. (1963) reported on the question of whether malignant melanoma is hereditary.
SCHOCH (1963) reported a pedigree study and a cytogenetic study of familial malignant melanoma.
TURKINGTON (1965) reported a familial factor in malignant melanoma.
Katzenellenbogen and Sandbank (1966) reported malignant melanomas in twins.
Smith et al. (1966) reported on familial melanoma.
Anderson et al. (1967) discussed hereditary aspects of malignant melanoma.
Lynch and Krush (1968) discussed heredity in malignant melanoma and its implications for early cancer detection.
Andrews (1968) reported malignant melanoma in siblings.
Anderson (1971) described the clinical characteristics of the genetic variety of cutaneous melanoma in man.
Wallace et al. (1971) addressed a genetic factor in malignant melanoma.
Robinson (1972) reported on familial occurrence of melanoma.
Wallace et al. (1973) reported on familial malignant melanoma.

Reimer et al. (1978) studied 7 consecutive melanoma-prone families. Pigmented lesions with distinctive clinical and histologic characteristics were present in 18 of 20 melanoma patients (90%) and in 24 of 43 first-degree relatives (56%). Recognising these lesions led to the detection of early-stage melanoma in 6 family members.

Reimer et al. (1978) concluded that the precursor-lesion syndrome in melanoma-prone families appeared to be an autosomal dominant trait. They suggested that it may serve as a cutaneous marker to identify persons at high risk for melanoma.

Greene et al. (1978) suggested that familial occurrences of malignant melanoma may be related to an inherited syndrome of precursor cutaneous lesions with distinct clinical and histologic features. They noted that recognizing this syndrome in relatives of melanoma patients identifies a subset of family members at high risk for melanoma, which makes early diagnosis and treatment easier.

Clark et al. (1978) described distinctive melanocytic moles in 37 patients from 6 melanoma families, designating the clinical and histologic features the 'B-K mole syndrome.' Among examined family members, 15 of 17 patients with melanoma and 22 of 41 nonmelanoma relatives had the unique moles.

Clark et al. (1978) reported that B-K mole syndrome was characterized clinically by fewer than 10 to more than 100 moles, prominent on the upper trunk and extremities, varying in size (5 to 15 mm), outline, and color. Histologically, B-K moles showed atypical melanocytic hyperplasia, lymphocytic infiltration, delicate fibroplasia, and new blood vessels occurring within a compound nevus or de novo.
Clark et al. (1978) photographically documented the transformation of 2 B-K moles into malignant melanomas, supporting the origin of familial melanomas from heritable melanocytic lesions.

Lynch et al. (1978) described a family showing concordance for malignant melanoma and a cutaneous phenotype characterized by multiple large moles of variable size and color (reddish-brown to bright red) with pigmentary leakage, which they termed the familial atypical multiple mole-melanoma syndrome. They suggested that this cutaneous phenotype signifies melanoma risk.

Lynch et al. (1978) found that transmission of the atypical multiple mole cutaneous phenotype in the reported family, and in several other families under investigation, was consistent with a simple autosomal dominant factor.
Greene et al. (1980) proposed a nomenclature for precursor naevi in cutaneous malignant melanoma.

Lynch et al. (1980) carried out clinical, pathologic, and genetic studies of 3 kindreds with the familial atypical multiple mole-melanoma (FAMMM) syndrome. Clinical expression varied widely, from apparent absence of disease through minimal, moderate, and florid manifestations; at the extreme, one patient had 9 separate primary melanomas over 18 years.

Lynch et al. (1980) found that the FAMMM moles were, on histology, compound nevocellular nevi showing variable melanocytic dysplasia, more frequent fibroplasia, and chronic inflammation in the papillary dermis. The degree of dysplasia varied markedly both between and within families.

Lynch et al. (1980) observed vertical transmission of cutaneous malignant melanoma and/or FAMMM moles, including father-to-son transmission, with no sex predilection. They concluded that the findings were consistent with an autosomal dominant gene with markedly variable expressivity.

Lynch et al. (1980) noted that managing these patients is difficult because it is not possible to know which moles need biopsy, or which will need wider excision after histologic study. They stressed that patients have a lifelong susceptibility to multiple malignant melanomas and suggested that cancers at other anatomic sites might be integral components of the syndrome.

Elder et al. (1980) reviewed clinical photographs of 79 prospectively studied cases of nonfamilial cutaneous malignant melanoma. Of these, 15 patients had moles on the covered buttock area. Seven of the 15 had large, clinically atypical nevi, and biopsies of these nevi showed severe melanocytic dysplasia. Residual elements of melanocytic dysplasia were found in 5 of the primary melanomas in this group.

Elder et al. (1980) suggested that patients with nonfamilial melanoma and dysplastic nevi have a distinct syndrome, which they called the dysplastic nevus syndrome (DNS), and that these patients are at increased risk of developing primary cutaneous malignant melanoma. The dysplastic nevi in these patients were identical to the precursor lesion of melanoma that the authors had previously described in families with the B-K mole syndrome. The authors stated that this was the first description of this form of dysplasia in nonfamilial melanoma.

Elder et al. (1980) introduced the term 'dysplastic nevus syndrome' (DNS) for sporadic, nonfamilial melanoma that occurs with dysplastic nevi. They described it as the counterpart of the familial B-K mole syndrome.
Hawkins et al. (1981) reported evidence for linkage between HLA and malignant melanoma.

Pellegris et al. (1982) did HLA-A, -B, and -C typing in 6 families with familial malignant melanoma (FMM). The HLA-B12 antigen was present in 5 of the 6 families. HLA-FMM linkage could be analyzed in 3 families: linkage was possible in 2 of them but not in the third.

Pellegris et al. (1982) suggested that there may be two types of familial malignant melanoma: a more frequent type, seen in 5 of 6 families, that apparently segregates with the HLA complex, and another type, seen in 1 family, that does not. They proposed that a factor in or linked to the HLA region played a role in 5 families, while another factor played that role in the sixth family.

Pellegris et al. (1982) concluded that their findings were consistent with the hypothesis that 2 complementary factors, one of them in the HLA complex, promote familial malignant melanoma with dominant inheritance and high penetrance.
Happle et al. (1982) presented arguments in favor of polygenic inheritance of precursor nevi.
Elder et al. (1982) gave their definition of the dysplastic nevus syndrome.
Kraemer et al. (1983) wrote about dysplastic nevi in relation to the risk of cutaneous melanoma.

Greene et al. (1983) did segregation analyses in 14 high-risk kindreds with multiple cases of cutaneous malignant melanoma (CMM) and the dysplastic nevus syndrome (DNS). They collected data on 401 family members. Pedigree analysis fit an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance for the familial CMM trait. A similar model probably also applied to DNS, but segregation analysis could not confirm a major locus for it.

Greene et al. (1983) did linkage analysis with 23 genetic markers in 14 kindreds with familial melanoma and dysplastic nevus syndrome. The results suggested that an autosomal dominant model was appropriate for DNS. They also suggested that a DNS/CMM susceptibility gene may lie on the short arm of chromosome 1, within 30 map units of the Rh locus, with a maximum lod score of 2.00.

Pathak et al. (1983) studied the karyotypes of 9 established human malignant melanoma cell lines from 2 female and 6 male patients. Every line had an aneuploid stemline chromosome number, and G-banding showed that chromosome 6 was involved in marker chromosomes in all of them. When the authors added previously reported cases, 38 of 47 karyotyped cell lines or primary melanoma cells (80.8%) had a marker chromosome involving chromosome 6.

Pathak et al. (1983) proposed that a genetic factor controlling melanoma initiation lies in the distal segment of 6q. They suggested that losing this segment, or all of 6q, makes a melanoblast or melanocyte malignant. They also noted that the proximal segment of 6q and 6p can take part in marker chromosome formation.

Lynch et al. (1983) described the familial atypical multiple mole-melanoma syndrome (FAMMM) as an autosomal dominantly inherited susceptibility to multiple atypical moles. The moles ranged in colour from black to brown, tan, red, or pink and were occasionally variegated. These compound naevi could be macular or papular with regular or irregular borders, measured 1 cm or more, and were found mainly on areas not exposed to the sun. Their number ranged from none to more than 100 per patient, and they had a propensity to transform to cutaneous malignant melanoma.

Lynch et al. (1983) reported that the histopathology of FAMMM naevi showed dysplastic changes in melanocytes, fibroplasia, focal chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate, and new blood vessel formation in the papillary dermis. These findings were not present in every lesion.

In a single FAMMM kindred, Lynch et al. (1983) observed that some members had minimal or absent cutaneous expression of the phenotype, and that the family had a more diverse range of neoplasms. The authors attributed this to pleiotropic effects of the cancer-prone FAMMM genotype.
Becher et al. (1983) performed cytogenetic analysis of malignant melanoma cells from a number of cases and found that chromosome 6 was frequently involved in structural aberrations.

Trent et al. (1983) performed chromosome banding analysis on 5 cases of human malignant melanoma. They found a variety of chromosome alterations, including deletion or translocation of chromosome 6q in 4 of the 5 cases. Comparing their results with previously published studies, the authors suggested that chromosome 6q may be a specific site of chromosome aberration in malignant melanoma.

Becher et al. (1983) analyzed chromosome aberrations in short-term cultures of 4 malignant melanomas using Giemsa banding. One tumor was near-diploid and three were near-triploid, and the authors identified 27 abnormal chromosomes, mostly translocations, followed by deletions and isochromosomes. Every case had markers derived from chromosomes 1 and 6, and three cases had abnormalities of chromosome 7. Each marker was unique to its case. Drawing on these results and on earlier reports, the authors suggested that abnormalities of chromosomes 6 and 7 may be characteristic of melanoma. They proposed that chromosome 1 aberrations may be a general feature of human neoplasia.

Howell et al. (1984) found that skin fibroblasts from 5 patients with hereditary cutaneous malignant melanoma and the dysplastic nevus syndrome were all more sensitive than normal to killing by the UV-mimetic carcinogen 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4NQO), with survival curves 2- to 3-fold steeper. Only 1 strain was hypersensitive to killing by broad-spectrum simulated sunlight (Sun Lamp radiation).

Howell et al. (1984) tested 2 of the fibroblast strains for mutagenicity at the 6-thioguanine-resistance locus: both were hypermutable after exposure to 4NQO, but only 1 showed a higher than normal frequency of mutants induced by simulated sunlight, paralleling each strain's cytotoxic response. The authors suggested that hypersensitivity to mutagens contributes to melanoma risk in these patients, supporting the somatic cell mutation hypothesis for the origin of cancer.

Balaban et al. (1984) performed chromosome studies on melanocytic lesions from 17 patients: 5 nevi (3 dysplastic), 1 early primary melanoma in radial growth phase, 1 advanced primary melanoma with multiple metastases, and 10 metastatic lesions. The nevi had normal karyotypes and each tumor had a predominantly abnormal karyotype. The early melanoma was pseudodiploid and had a 6p;22 translocation.

Balaban et al. (1984) found that 10 of 11 advanced melanomas had aberrations of chromosome 1. In 9 of them, deletions or translocations of 1p involved the proximal segment 1p12-1p22 9 times in 8 lesions. Six advanced tumors had extra 7q material (4 with extra copies of chromosome 7 and 2 with 7q+). Nine melanomas had chromosome 6 alterations, including 3 with extra copies of 6p. The authors suggested that genes important in melanoma carcinogenesis are located on proximal 1p, on 7q, and on chromosome 6.

Balaban et al. (1984) studied one advanced tumor in which the primary lesion and 5 metastases, removed one after another over 18 months, had nearly identical karyotypes. They concluded that this showed the neoplasm was clonal.

Ochi et al. (1984) carried out cytogenetic studies of a metastatic malignant melanoma from a 54-year-old white woman on 3 separate occasions. They found 2 different clones, one hypodiploid and one hypertriploid, and both had the same marker chromosomes, der(6)t(6;17) and der(17)t(1;17). Based on the histopathology and clinical course, the authors suggested that the 2 clones reflected different morphology and the results of therapy.
Arndt (1984) discussed congenital nevi and dysplastic nevi as precursors to malignant melanoma.

Rey et al. (1985) performed G-banding cytogenetic analysis on direct and in vitro preparations of a malignant melanoma that had spread to the brain. The tumor had a pseudodiploid modal chromosome number and 5 marker chromosomes, one of which was an i(6p). The authors stated that this result agreed with earlier reports that chromosome 6 is preferentially involved in malignant melanoma.
Greene et al. (1985) described the familial dysplastic nevus syndrome and characterized dysplastic nevi as acquired precursors of cutaneous malignant melanoma.

Bale et al. (1985) performed detailed HLA typing in 11 families with hereditary cutaneous malignant melanoma (CMM) and dysplastic nevi. They also re-analyzed previously published data from 19 other families. In the pooled data from all 30 families, with CMM defined as the trait, linkage to HLA was rejected for all recombination fractions (theta) below 40%. When the combined CMM/dysplastic nevus trait was analyzed in 18 families, there was strong evidence against linkage to the major histocompatibility complex.

Bale et al. (1985) found significant heterogeneity when they compared different subgroups of families in the HLA linkage analysis. They suggested that preferential reporting of positive linkage results and misclassification of subjects' CMM susceptibility status may have contributed to the earlier belief that the hereditary melanoma gene was linked to HLA.
Bale et al. (1985) described dysplastic nevi as a well-characterized precursor of hereditary cutaneous malignant melanoma.

Rhodes et al. (1985) studied 39 probands with small (less than 40 mm) congenital nevomelanocytic nevi (CNN). The probands were registered by photograph in 1982 at a children's hospital dermatology service. Of the probands' 65 sibs, 8 (12.3%) also had one or more small CNN. This rate is 11 times the 1.1% prevalence of CNN in newborn infants reported by a survey of newborns in the same city. In 5 of the 39 families, an affected parent with CNN was also found.

Rhodes et al. (1985) concluded that small congenital nevomelanocytic nevi may aggregate in families. They suggested that either autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance or multifactorial determination could explain this.

Using a life-table and disease-free survival analysis approach, Bale et al. (1986) estimated the lifetime incidence of melanoma in sibs and offspring of individuals affected with dysplastic nevi (DN) to be 46%, consistent with a highly penetrant autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.

Bale et al. (1986) performed linkage analysis between the melanoma locus and a hypothetical DN locus and obtained a maximum lod score of 3.857 at theta = 0.08; all families giving evidence for linkage were in coupling phase and the maximum likelihood estimate of theta was not significantly different from 0 (P = 0.1). The authors concluded that the DN and melanoma traits may represent pleiotropic effects of a single highly penetrant autosomal dominant gene.

Kopf et al. (1986) used consecutive questionnaires completed prospectively on 1,169 patients with cutaneous malignant melanoma. Of these, 69 patients reported a family history of melanoma. Compared with nonfamilial cases, familial melanoma was significantly associated with younger age at first diagnosis, smaller lesion diameter, lower Clark level, less frequent nonmelanoma skin cancer, and lower prevalence of noncutaneous cancer. The authors suggested that greater awareness of melanoma among family members could explain some of these observations.

Bale and Chakravarti (1987) reported evidence for autosomal dominant inheritance of a cutaneous malignant melanoma (CMM)/dysplastic nevus (DN) gene, and for pleiotropy of that gene, meaning that one gene accounts for both CMM and DN.

Dracopoli et al. (1987) screened RFLPs at 61 autosomal and 7 X-linked loci in cell lines from 6 independent metastases and autologous B cells from a patient with melanoma. Loss of heterozygosity was found in tumor cells at 8 of 16 informative autosomes and at all 3 informative X-linked loci, generally without karyotypic abnormalities in the affected regions.

Dracopoli et al. (1987) found that all 6 metastases shared inactivation of the same X chromosome and identical segregations at loci on chromosomes 9 and X, supporting monoclonal origin. From the patterns of loss, they built a genealogy of tumor progression and a model in which metastatic cells accumulate selectively neutral and advantageous segregations.
Hartley et al. (1987) described 7 cases of malignant melanoma in close relatives of children with osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma.

Hartley et al. (1987) discussed an association between malignant melanoma and certain childhood cancers: adrenal cortical carcinoma, osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma and retinoblastoma. They proposed that in certain families, melanoma may be another manifestation of the same gene defect that causes susceptibility to the tumors characteristic of the SBLA cancer family syndrome.
Pascoe (1987) discussed the inheritance of cutaneous malignant melanoma (CMM) and dysplastic nevus syndrome (DNS).
Hecht (1989) reviewed the 1820 description by Norris of hereditary malignant melanoma of the skin.

Vasen et al. (1989) studied 9 families with the dysplastic nevus syndrome identified since 1982 in the Leiden area of the Netherlands. In these families, 38 persons had a total of 50 primary melanomas. Nineteen melanomas were diagnosed before a screening programme began, 11 were found at the first examination of the families, and 20 were found during follow-up.

Vasen et al. (1989) found that melanomas detected by screening in families with dysplastic nevus syndrome were at an earlier stage. Melanoma in situ made up 1 of 19 melanomas diagnosed before screening, 2 of 11 found at the first examination, and 7 of 20 found during follow-up. The mean thickness of invasive melanomas in these 3 groups was 1.75, 0.80, and 0.54 mm. Sixteen of 19 pre-screening melanomas (84%) were Clark level III or IV, compared with 15 of 20 follow-up melanomas (75%) that were Clark level I or II. The authors concluded that screening can lead to earlier detection, curative treatment, and better prognosis, and they discussed the need for central registration of affected families.

Bale et al. (1989) studied 99 relatives and 26 spouses in 6 families with a predisposition to melanoma. Analysis of cosegregation of the cutaneous malignant melanoma-dysplastic nevus trait with 26 polymorphic DNA markers on chromosome 1p placed a melanoma susceptibility gene between the anonymous marker D1S47 and the pronatrodilatin gene (PND) in band 1p36, with odds greater than 260,000:1 in favor of linkage.

In the 6 melanoma-prone families studied by Bale et al. (1989), 34 family members had cutaneous malignant melanoma, 31 of whom also had histologically confirmed dysplastic nevi; another 24 family members had dysplastic nevi alone.

Dracopoli et al. (1989) examined loci on chromosome 1p for loss of constitutional heterozygosity in 35 melanomas and 21 melanoma cell lines. They found loss of heterozygosity at 1p loci in 15 of 35 (43%) melanomas and 11 of 21 (52%) melanoma cell lines.

Dracopoli et al. (1989) analyzed multiple metastases from the same patient, and melanoma and lymphoblastoid samples from a family with hereditary melanoma. They concluded that loss of heterozygosity at distal 1p is a late event in tumor progression rather than the second mutation expected if melanoma arose by a cellular recessive mechanism. Based on comparisons with neuroblastoma and MEN2, they suggested that frequent 1p LOH is a common late event in the progression of neuroectodermal tumors.

Traupe et al. (1989) estimated mutation rates to test whether the dysplastic nevus syndrome associated with familial melanoma is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. The mutation rate estimated directly from sporadic occurrence was exceedingly high (0.9%-2.5%). The rate estimated with Haldane's formula was 0.007% to 0.02%. From these figures the authors calculated that newly arising mutations would outnumber eliminated mutations by 100:1, so that within a few generations 10% of the world population would be affected. They concluded that this apparent lack of genetic equilibrium is not compatible with autosomal dominant inheritance of the dysplastic nevus syndrome.

Cannon-Albright et al. (1990) studied 3 Utah kindreds ascertained for multiple cases of melanoma and genotyped family members for PND and D1S47, the 2 markers on distal 1p reported by Bale et al. as most closely linked. They found no evidence for linkage whether they analyzed melanoma alone or a combined melanoma/dysplastic nevus syndrome phenotype. Multipoint linkage analysis excluded the CM/DNS locus from a 55-cM region containing the PND-D1S47 interval.
Cannon-Albright et al. (1990) suggested that diagnostic or genetic heterogeneity could explain why they found no linkage to 1p36 in Utah melanoma kindreds when Bale et al. had reported linkage there.

Kefford et al. (1991) studied 119 members of 8 newly described Australian families with hereditary melanoma. Thirty had cutaneous malignant melanoma, and only 8 of these also had dysplastic nevi. Another 15 family members had dysplastic nevi without melanoma. The pedigrees fell into 3 groups: hereditary melanoma with no associated dysplastic nevi, hereditary melanoma with occasional affected individuals who had dysplastic nevi, and hereditary melanoma with dysplastic nevi.
Kefford et al. (1991) found an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance in all 8 Australian families with hereditary melanoma.

Kefford et al. (1991) tested whether the melanoma/dysplastic nevus trait cosegregated with 8 polymorphic DNA markers on chromosome 1p, including the distal markers D1S47 and PND. They obtained a strongly negative probability of linkage, which effectively excluded the putative melanoma susceptibility gene in these 8 Australian families from the distal 1p region. No other chromosome 1 marker they tested showed linkage. The authors suggested that hereditary melanoma is heterogeneous both in its genetic basis and in its association with the dysplastic nevus syndrome.

Millikin et al. (1991) used RFLP analysis with 5 markers on 6q and 1 on 6p to study 20 paired tumor and normal DNA samples from patients with malignant melanoma, and found loss of heterozygosity on 6q at 21 of 53 informative loci (40%). Five patients had allele losses consistent with loss of the entire 6q arm or of an entire chromosome 6, and 4 others had terminal 6q deletions.

Millikin et al. (1991) found that the region with the highest frequency of 6q allelic loss (60%) in melanoma was defined by the marker loci c-MYB and ESR (6q22-23 and 6q24-27), whereas LOH at loci on chromosomes 1, 11, 16, and 17 was observed in only 5% of cases. They concluded that loss of 6q sequences is a nonrandom and possibly biologically relevant event in human malignant melanoma.

Fountain et al. (1992) performed loss-of-heterozygosity studies in melanoma using 8 markers spanning 9pter to proximal 9q (D9S33, IFNB1, the IFNA gene cluster, D9S126, D9S3, D9S19, GGTB2, and ASSP3). Two or more loci were hemizygously reduced in 12 of 14 (86%) informative metastatic melanoma tumor and cell line DNAs, and homozygous deletions of D9S126 were observed in 2 of 20 (10%) melanoma cell lines, defining a small critical region of 2-3 Mb on 9p21 in which a putative melanoma tumor-suppressor gene was likely to reside.

Fountain et al. (1992) eliminated several 9p candidate genes, including IFNB1, the IFNA gene cluster, GGTB2, and the TYRP locus, as targets of the melanoma tumor-suppressor locus because they lie outside the homozygously deleted regions.

Nancarrow et al. (1992) carried out linkage studies between chromosome 1p markers and familial melanoma in 7 Australian kindreds, 3 of which were the largest reported worldwide. They excluded a melanoma gene from a 40-cM region spanning the interval between D1S47 and PND and extending about 15 cM on either side of these markers. They also excluded a region of about 20 cM around the MYCL1/D1S57 loci.

Nancarrow et al. (1992) noted that there was considerable controversy over whether a cutaneous malignant melanoma/dysplastic nevus gene (CMM) maps to distal 1p, linked to PND and D1S47. They stated that no study had found support for linkage of familial melanoma alone to these markers. Their own linkage data from 7 Australian kindreds excluded this region.

Goldstein et al. (1993) studied markers D1S47, PND, and D1S160 on chromosome 1p in 7 new families (set B) and updated versions of 6 previously reported families (set A) with cutaneous malignant melanoma-dysplastic nevus (CMM/DN). When only CMM was considered affected, a maximum lod score of 3.12 at theta = 0.10 was obtained with D1S47 and 1.76 at theta = 0.10 with D1S160, whereas PND showed no evidence for linkage. Under CMM/DN models, strong evidence for linkage to D1S47, D1S160, and PND was found in the set A pedigrees but not in the set B families.

Goldstein et al. (1993) found significant evidence for genetic heterogeneity of CMM/DN when families were split by the proportion of CMM/DN cases (with D1S47 and D1S160) and by the occurrence of immune-related tumors (with D1S160), with only a subset of families appearing linked to chromosome 1p. They concluded that diagnostic, clinical, and genetic heterogeneity likely explained previous failures to confirm 1p linkage.

Goldstein et al. (1996) carried out two-trait-locus, two-marker-locus linkage analysis in 19 cutaneous malignant melanoma/dysplastic nevi (CMM/DN) kindreds that had earlier shown significant evidence of linkage and heterogeneity to both chromosomes 1p and 9p. For CMM alone, the highest LOD score was obtained with a single-locus heterogeneity model (Z = 8.48 at theta = 0.0), and evidence for linkage was much stronger for 9p than for 1p, with LOD scores about 2 times greater on 9p. After conditioning on linkage to the other locus, only the 9p locus consistently showed significant evidence of linkage to CMM alone.

Goldstein et al. (1996) found that LOD scores changed when the phenotype was CMM/DN rather than CMM alone. They suggested that a chromosome 1p locus (or loci) contributed to both CMM and CMM/DN, whereas a 9p locus contributed more to CMM alone. Under both 2-locus models, 1p LOD scores were higher for CMM/DN than for CMM alone (epistatic: 4.63 vs 3.83; heterogeneity: 4.94 vs 3.80). In contrast, 9p LOD scores were substantially lower for CMM/DN than for CMM alone (epistatic: 4.64 vs 7.06; heterogeneity: 5.38 vs 7.99). Five of the kindreds showed evidence of linkage (Z > 0.7) to both regions.
Gilchrest et al. (1999) reviewed the pathogenesis of melanoma induced by ultraviolet radiation.

Hejny et al. (2001) described 7 patients who developed retinopathy while receiving high-dose interferon alfa-2b as adjuvant treatment for high-risk melanoma. In 5 patients, visual acuity was normal, they had cotton-wool spots and/or retinal hemorrhages, and the retinopathy resolved after treatment was stopped. The other 2 patients developed severe retinopathy with vision loss to counting fingers or hand motions, and their retinopathy did not resolve. The retinopathy was detected after 6 to 26 weeks of maintenance treatment, at total doses of 816 to 1770 million units. The authors concluded that the risk appeared to be greater with higher doses and that patients should be monitored until the retinopathy resolves to screen for sequelae such as retinal neovascularization.

Noonan et al. (2001) used a genetically engineered mouse model to show that a single dose of burning ultraviolet radiation given to neonates, but not to adults, was necessary and sufficient to induce tumors resembling human melanoma, with high penetrance. The authors concluded that their results provided experimental support for epidemiologic evidence that childhood sunburn poses a significant risk of developing melanoma.

In a systematic screen of signaling pathway genes in human cancer, Davies et al. (2002) found somatic missense mutations in the BRAF gene in 66% of malignant melanomas, and at lower frequency in a wide range of other human cancers. All mutations were within the kinase domain, and a single substitution, V599E, accounted for 80% of them.

Davies et al. (2002) showed that mutated BRAF proteins had elevated kinase activity and transformed NIH3T3 cells. RAS function was not required for the growth of cancer cell lines carrying the V599E mutation. The authors suggested that BRAF may provide new therapeutic opportunities in malignant melanoma.

Potter et al. (2002) described a 32-year-old woman with a history of metastatic melanoma who developed melanoma-associated retinopathy, with reduced vision in both eyes. Electroretinography showed a 'negative' B-wave, and Goldmann perimetry showed paracentral and central scotomas. Western blotting of her serum showed antibodies to retinal transducin, but immunohistochemistry found no immunoreactivity to retinal bipolar cells. The authors concluded that melanoma-associated retinopathy can be related to a variety of antiretinal antibodies and identified transducin as a novel antigen in this condition.

Tucker et al. (2002) followed 33 melanoma-prone families, each with more than 2 living members with invasive melanoma, for up to 25 years. A total of 844 family members were examined and photographed, and melanocytic lesions were photographed in sequence and examined histologically when removed. All of the families had members with dysplastic nevi and melanoma. Most dysplastic nevi stayed stable or regressed, and few changed in a way that should raise concern for melanoma. The authors concluded that with careful surveillance, melanomas can be found early.

Of the 33 melanoma-prone families studied by Tucker et al. (2002), 17 had germline CDKN2A mutations, 2 had CDK4 mutations, and 14 had no mutation identified in either gene. The melanomas and dysplastic nevi in these families did not appear to differ by the type of mutation identified.

Pollock et al. (2003) performed mutation analysis on microdissected melanoma and nevus samples. They found BRAF mutations causing the V599E amino acid substitution in 41 of 60 (68%) melanoma metastases, 4 of 5 (80%) primary melanomas, and, unexpectedly, 63 of 77 (82%) nevi. The authors suggested that mutational activation of the RAS/RAF/MAPK pathway in nevi is a critical step in starting melanocytic neoplasia but is not enough on its own to cause melanoma.

Fung et al. (2003) described eMelanoBase, an online locus-specific database set up by the international Melanoma Genetics Consortium. It collects germline variants seen in all loci implicated in familial melanoma susceptibility, mainly CDKN2A and, rarely, CDK4. The core dataset records nucleotide variants at the genomic and transcript levels, amino acid variants, and citations. The ancillary dataset records keyword descriptions of effects on transcription and translation, along with epidemiologic data.

Fung et al. (2003) noted that the CDKN2A locus encodes 2 unrelated proteins from alternatively spliced transcripts read in different frames. The alpha transcript (exons 1-alpha, 2, and 3) produces p16INK4A, and the beta transcript (exons 1-beta and 2) produces p14ARF. They stated that exon 2 mutations can impair both proteins. They also stated that insertions and deletions in exons 1-alpha, 1-beta, and 2 could in theory produce p16INK4A-p14ARF fusion proteins, which existing databases did not take into account.

Gillanders et al. (2003) ran a genomewide linkage scan in 49 Australian pedigrees, each with at least 3 cases of cutaneous malignant melanoma, in which CDKN2A and CDK4 involvement had been excluded. The highest 2-point parametric lod score was 1.82 (theta = 0.2) at D1S2726 on 1p22. In 9 families selected for early age at onset, the parametric lod score was 4.65 (theta = 0) and the nonparametric lod score was 4.19 at D1S2779. Additional typing in this subset gave 7 adjacent markers with lod scores above 3, with the highest parametric lod score of 4.95 (theta = 0) and a nonparametric lod score of 5.37 at D1S2776.

Gillanders et al. (2003) analyzed 33 additional multiplex melanoma families from several continents and found further evidence for linkage to 1p22, again strongest in families with the earliest mean age at diagnosis. In a nonparametric ordered sequential analysis based on the average age at diagnosis in each family, the highest lod score was 6.43 at D1S2779, reached when the 15 families with the earliest ages at onset were included. The authors concluded that there was significant evidence for a novel melanoma susceptibility gene in chromosome band 1p22.

Gillanders et al. (2003) noted that mutations in CDKN2A and CDK4 account for only 20 to 25% of families with multiple cases of cutaneous malignant melanoma. They pointed to additional susceptibility loci and localized one to 1p22 in families without CDKN2A or CDK4 involvement.

Alexander et al. (2004) studied contrast sensitivity in 2 patients with melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR), aged 57 and 61 years, who had normal Snellen visual acuity. Both patients had lower contrast sensitivity than 10 normal observers. With the steady-pedestal paradigm (presumed to reflect the magnocellular pathway), the loss was greatest at the lowest spatial frequency (0.25 cpd). With the pulsed-pedestal paradigm (presumed to reflect the parvocellular pathway), the loss was greatest at 1 cpd. Sensitivity was normal at 8 cpd. The authors concluded that the deficits were not specific to the magnocellular pathway. They said the deficits instead depended on spatial frequency and were consistent with retinal bipolar cell dysfunction.

Curtin et al. (2005) compared genome-wide DNA copy-number changes and BRAF and N-RAS mutation status in 126 melanomas. The tumors fell into 4 groups with different ultraviolet exposure: 30 from skin with chronic sun-induced damage, 40 from skin without such damage, 36 acral, and 20 mucosal. The 4 groups differed significantly in regional copy-number changes and BRAF mutation frequencies. Copy-number changes alone classified the samples into the 4 groups with 70% accuracy, separated the 2 sun-exposure groups with 84% accuracy, and separated acral from mucosal melanoma with 89% accuracy.

Curtin et al. (2005) found somatic BRAF or N-RAS mutations in 81% of melanomas from skin without chronic sun-induced damage. Most melanomas from chronically sun-damaged skin, acral sites, and mucosal sites had mutations in neither gene.

Curtin et al. (2005) found that melanomas without BRAF or N-RAS mutations often had increased copy numbers of CDK4 and CCND1, which act downstream in the RAS-BRAF pathway. They concluded that melanoma develops through distinct genetic pathways, and that CDK4 and CCND1 are implicated as independent oncogenes in melanomas lacking BRAF or N-RAS mutations.

Zhang et al. (2006) used high-resolution array-based comparative genomic hybridization to analyze 283 known human miRNA genes in 227 ovarian cancer, breast cancer, and melanoma specimens. Copy number alterations, counted as significant when present in more than 15% of tumors, were found at 85.9% of miRNA-containing genomic loci in melanoma, compared with 72.8% in breast cancer and 37.1% in ovarian cancer. Forty-one miRNA genes had copy number changes shared by all 3 cancer types (26 gains and 15 losses), and miRNA copy number changes correlated with miRNA expression.

Zhang et al. (2006) found frequent copy number abnormalities of DICER1, Argonaute-2, and other miRNA-associated genes in melanoma and in breast and ovarian cancer. They suggested that copy number changes in miRNAs and their regulatory genes may partly explain the frequent miRNA deregulation seen in tumors.

Constantinescu et al. (2007) identified 5 cases of malignant melanoma in the DATATOP clinical trial cohort of patients with early Parkinson disease, compared with 1.5 expected for a standard healthy population, giving a standardized event ratio of 3.3 (95% CI, 1.1-7.8), indicating that the incidence of melanoma was higher than expected. They found no association between levodopa therapy and melanoma incidence.

Ferreira et al. (2007) carried out a cross-sectional survey of 150 Parkinson disease patients and 146 age-matched controls, each examined by a dermatologist. Neoplastic or preneoplastic skin lesions were found in 35 PD patients (23.3%) and 20 controls (13.7%) (OR 1.92; 95% CI 1.05-3.51). The difference was no longer significant after adjusting for gender. Among the PD patients, 29 (19%) had actinic keratosis and 4 (3%) had basal cell carcinoma. The authors judged the results nonconclusive but consistent with an increased risk of skin cancer in PD. Citing the melanoma risk linked to actinic keratosis, they recommended screening for it in future epidemiologic studies.

Schatton et al. (2008) identified a subpopulation of cells enriched for human malignant-melanoma-initiating cells (MMIC), defined by expression of the chemoresistance mediator ABCB5. ABCB5+ tumour cells found in human melanoma patients had a primitive molecular phenotype and correlated with clinical melanoma progression.

In serial human-to-mouse xenotransplantation experiments, Schatton et al. (2008) found that ABCB5+ melanoma cells had greater tumorigenic capacity than ABCB5- bulk populations and re-established clinical tumour heterogeneity. In vivo genetic lineage tracking showed that ABCB5+ cells produced both ABCB5+ and ABCB5- progeny, which indicated self-renewal and differentiation. ABCB5- populations gave rise, at lower rates, only to ABCB5- cells.

In an initial proof-of-principle analysis, Schatton et al. (2008) gave a monoclonal antibody directed at ABCB5 systemically. The antibody could induce antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity in ABCB5+ melanoma-initiating cells, and it inhibited tumour growth. The authors suggested that MMIC are also required for the growth of established tumours.

In European populations comprising 2,121 individuals with cutaneous melanoma, 2,163 with basal cell carcinoma, and over 40,000 controls, Gudbjartsson et al. (2008) found that a haplotype near ASIP, known to affect a similar spectrum of pigmentation traits as MC1R variants, conferred significant risk of cutaneous melanoma (OR = 1.45, P = 1.2 x 10(-9)) and BCC (OR = 1.33, P = 1.2 x 10(-6)). The association was robust to adjustment for the effect of pigmentation.

Gudbjartsson et al. (2008) found that the TYR variant encoding the R402Q amino acid substitution, previously shown to affect eye color and tanning response, conferred risk of cutaneous melanoma (OR = 1.21, P = 2.8 x 10(-7)) and basal cell carcinoma (OR = 1.14, P = 6.1 x 10(-4)) in European case-control populations, robust to adjustment for pigmentation.

Gudbjartsson et al. (2008) found that an eye color variant in TYRP1 was associated with risk of cutaneous melanoma (OR = 1.15, P = 4.6 x 10(-4)) in European populations, robust to adjustment for pigmentation.

In a Spanish case-control study of 131 consecutive melanoma patients and 245 controls frequency-matched for sex and age, Fernandez et al. (2008) genotyped 23 SNPs in 6 pigmentation pathway genes. They found that the variant allele of the c.1122C>G (p.Phe374Leu; rs16891982) SNP in SLC45A2 (MATP) was associated with protection from malignant melanoma (OR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.24-0.70; P = 0.008 after adjustment for multiple testing).

Fernandez et al. (2008) supported the protective association of the SLC45A2 p.Phe374Leu variant allele by showing that it was consistently linked with dark hair, dark skin, dark eye color, solar lentigines, and childhood sunburns. They stated that this was the first time SLC45A2 had been described as a melanoma susceptibility gene in a light-skinned population.

Rafnar et al. (2009) tested rs401681 at the TERT-CLPTM1L locus on chromosome 5p15.33. Its C allele was a risk allele for basal cell carcinoma and for lung, bladder, prostate and cervical cancer. In a sample set of 2,443 melanoma cases and 30,839 controls from Iceland, Sweden and Spain, rs401681(C) was significantly associated with protection against cutaneous melanoma (OR = 0.88, P = 8.0 x 10(-4)). The authors noted a published study reporting that long telomeres are associated with increased melanoma risk, whereas short telomeres are associated with increased risk of basal cell carcinoma.

Rafnar et al. (2009) found that rs401681 lies in an intron of the CLPTM1L gene and is in strong linkage disequilibrium with rs2736098, a synonymous SNP (Ala305Ala) in exon 2 of TERT. rs401681(C) was not associated with pigment phenotypes (hair and eye colour, freckling or Fitzpatrick skin type). It was also not associated with TERT or CLPTM1L RNA expression in whole blood or adipose tissue.

Gao et al. (2009) examined natural hair color in early adulthood and Parkinson disease (PD) risk in 38,641 men (Health Professionals Follow-up Study) and 93,661 women (Nurses' Health Study) in the US. Red hair is a risk factor for melanoma. PD risk rose as hair color became lighter. After adjusting for age, smoking, ethnicity and other covariates, the pooled relative risks were 1.40 for brown, 1.61 for blond and 1.93 for red hair compared with black hair. The association was strongest for PD onset before age 70 (relative risk 3.83 for red vs black hair).

In a case-control study nested in the same two cohorts (272 PD cases and 1,185 controls genotyped), Gao et al. (2009) found that homozygosity for the MC1R Arg151Cys loss-of-function variant was strongly associated with red hair (relative risk 57). The authors described this variant as the SNP most consistently associated with melanoma risk. Compared with Arg/Arg, the Cys/Cys genotype was associated with a higher PD risk (adjusted relative risk 3.15; 95% CI 1.06-9.37). The authors suggested that the shared links of both diseases to light hair color and this variant may partly explain why melanoma occurs more often in people with PD, rather than this being an adverse effect of levodopa.

Passeron et al. (2009) found that SOX9 was expressed in normal human skin but was increasingly downregulated as melanocytes progressed to premalignant, then malignant and metastatic states. Overexpression of SOX9 in human and mouse melanoma cell lines caused cell cycle arrest by increasing p21 transcription. It also restored sensitivity to retinoic acid by downregulating PRAME, a melanoma antigen.
Passeron et al. (2009) showed that overexpressing SOX9 in melanoma cell lines inhibited tumorigenicity both in mice and in a human ex vivo model of melanoma.

Passeron et al. (2009) found that treating melanoma cell lines with PGD2 increased SOX9 expression and restored sensitivity to retinoic acid. Combined treatment with PGD2 and retinoic acid substantially decreased tumor growth in human ex vivo and mouse in vivo melanoma models. The authors suggested this pointed to a possible noncytotoxic approach to treating melanoma.
In a letter, Herrero Hernández (2009) discussed pigmentation as a clue to understanding the relationship between Parkinson disease and melanoma.

Bishop et al. (2009) performed a genome-wide association study of melanoma in the GenoMEL consortium. It used 317K tagging SNPs in 1,650 selected cases and 4,336 controls of European ancestry. Replication was in 1,149 cases and 964 controls from GenoMEL and in a population-based case-control study from Leeds, UK, with 1,163 cases and 903 controls. Five loci reached P < 5 x 10(-7) in the genome-wide screen. Three were replicated: 16q24 encompassing MC1R, 11q14-q21 encompassing TYR, and 9p21 adjacent to MTAP and flanking CDKN2A.

Bishop et al. (2009) found that the strongest melanoma association was with a 16q24 region that includes MC1R, CDK10 and FANCA. For rs258322, the combined P value was 2.54 x 10(-27) and the per-allele odds ratio was 1.67 (95% CI 1.52-1.83). Stepwise regression showed association with three SNPs (rs258322, rs4785763, rs8059973). rs8059973 appeared to be associated with melanoma risk independently of the other two.

Bishop et al. (2009) found that a chromosome 11 region including TYR was associated with melanoma. The strongest overall evidence was for rs1393350 (P = 2.41 x 10(-14); OR 1.29). The TYR coding variant rs1126809 was also associated (OR 1.27, P = 1.17 x 10(-6)). After accounting for rs1393350, no other SNPs in the region were independently associated.

Bishop et al. (2009) replicated a 9p21 melanoma susceptibility locus. The SNP rs7023329, within the MTAP gene, reached an overall P value of 4.03 x 10(-7) (OR 0.85). Stepwise regression showed a second independent association with rs1011970, located 246 kb centromeric within ANRIL, which overlaps CDKN2B. The authors noted that common variants at this locus had not previously been associated with melanoma.

Bishop et al. (2009) also confirmed melanoma associations at two other regions. The first was a chromosome 20 region containing the pigmentation gene ASIP (rs1885120; OR 1.58, P = 1.25 x 10(-8)). The second was a chromosome 22 region previously identified in a GWAS of nevus count (rs2284063; overall P = 2.40 x 10(-9)).

Bishop et al. (2009) found no significant pairwise interactions between the top SNPs at the 9p21, 11q and 16q24 loci, which was consistent with a multiplicative model. Associations were similar across case categories (family history, multiple primaries and early onset). For some SNPs, the effect was marginally weaker in early-onset melanoma. Despite variation in allele frequency and sun exposure, effect sizes were notably homogeneous across European-ancestry populations living at different latitudes.

Falchi et al. (2009) performed a genome-wide association study of total body nevus count in 1,524 healthy adult female twins from the TwinsUK registry. They replicated the results in 4,107 adolescent subjects of European ancestry from the Brisbane Twin Nevus Study. The strongest association was with rs4636294, located in the 5-prime UTR of the MTAP gene on 9p21 next to CDKN2A (combined P = 3.4 x 10(-15)).

Falchi et al. (2009) found a second replicated locus for nevus count on 22q13.1. The strongest SNP there was rs2284063 (combined P = 3.4 x 10(-8)), which lies in the intron between exons 2 and 3 of PLA2G6. Each of the 9p21 and 22q13 loci explained roughly 0.7 to 3.0% of the variance in nevus count.

Falchi et al. (2009) reported that the effects of rs4636294 and rs2284063 on nevus count were additive. TwinsUK subjects homozygous for the risk alleles at both SNPs had more than twice as many nevi (median 30) as subjects homozygous for the protective alleles (median 12.5). Among Australian BTNS subjects, the corresponding medians were 116 and 79.

Falchi et al. (2009) tested the nevus-associated loci in 2 melanoma case-control samples: the Australian Q-MEGA study (1,734 cases) and the Leeds study from the UK (1,274 incident cases and 123 familial cases without CDKN2A mutations). Both loci were associated with melanoma. The strongest associations were rs10757257 at 9p21 (combined OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.15-1.30; P = 3.4 x 10(-8)) and rs132985 at 22q13 (combined OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.15-1.30; P = 2.6 x 10(-7)). In the Leeds sample, subjects homozygous for the risk alleles at both loci had about double the risk of melanoma (OR 1.94).

Falchi et al. (2009) used the Leeds nevus-count subsample (903 cases and 485 controls). When the SNP–melanoma association was adjusted for nevus count, the odds ratio for melanoma moved toward 1.0. The authors interpreted this as consistent with melanoma risk at these loci being mediated through nevus count.

Pleasance et al. (2010) sequenced the whole genome of COLO-829, a malignant melanoma cell line. It came from an untreated metastasis in a 43-year-old man with no identified skin primary. They compared it with a lymphoblastoid line (COLO-829BL) from the same patient. They identified 33,345 somatic base substitutions, 66 confirmed small insertions/deletions, and 37 confirmed somatic rearrangements. Of the base substitutions, 292 were in protein-coding sequences, and 187 of these were nonsynonymous.

Pleasance et al. (2010) found BRAF V600E and a 12-kb internal homozygous deletion of PTEN by genome-wide sequencing of the COLO-829 melanoma genome. They predicted that the PTEN deletion causes premature termination. A previously known 2-bp deletion in CDKN2A was not detected in the genome-wide calls but was found in sequence reads when a targeted search was made.

Pleasance et al. (2010) found that most somatic base substitutions in the COLO-829 melanoma were C-to-T/G-to-A transitions. Of 510 dinucleotide substitutions, 360 were CC-to-TT/GG-to-AA changes. In addition, 92% of C-to-T mutations occurred at the 3-prime base of a pyrimidine dinucleotide. The authors concluded that most of these substitutions were attributable to DNA damage from ultraviolet light.

Pleasance et al. (2010) found fewer C-to-T mutations on the transcribed strands than on the nontranscribed strands of genes (2,773 vs 4,058). Mutation prevalence was also lower over gene footprints, in exons, and in highly expressed genes. They interpreted this as evidence of transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair and of an additional form of repair preferentially directed at genic regions.

In a region of loss of heterozygosity on chromosome 1q in the COLO-829 melanoma, Pleasance et al. (2010) compared early (homozygous) with later (heterozygous) somatic substitutions. C-to-T mutations made up more of the early mutations (82%) than the late mutations (53%). C-to-A/G-to-T changes made up more of the late mutations (19% vs 2%). The authors suggested that ultraviolet exposure ended later in the tumor's evolution, perhaps at metastasis.

In the COLO-829 melanoma, Pleasance et al. (2010) identified two heterozygous somatic missense mutations in SPDEF, p.S229L and p.D283H. Sequencing SPDEF in 48 additional untreated metastatic melanomas revealed a further somatic mutation, p.W158*. The authors noted that additional melanomas would need to be analyzed to determine the significance of these mutations.

In the COLO-829 melanoma, Pleasance et al. (2010) also found a heterozygous missense mutation in MMP28 (p.G297E) and one in UVRAG (p.N561K). An exonic deletion in MAGI2 produced an expressed in-frame chimeric transcript of unclear significance. There were also high-level amplifications on chromosome 3p (including RARB and TOP2B) and on chromosome 15, and a homozygous deletion removing the start codon of CNOT1.

Flaherty et al. (2010) ran a multicenter phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PLX4032 (RG7204), an oral inhibitor of mutated BRAF, given twice daily. Of 55 patients in the dose-escalation phase, 49 had melanoma. Among the 16 patients whose melanomas carried the V600E BRAF mutation and who received 240 mg or more twice daily, 10 had a partial response and 1 had a complete response (69%). Responses occurred at all metastatic sites, including liver, small bowel, and bone, and lasted from 2 to more than 18 months.

Flaherty et al. (2010) treated an extension cohort of 32 patients with metastatic melanoma carrying the V600E BRAF mutation with PLX4032 at the recommended phase 2 dose of 960 mg twice daily. Of these, 26 (81%) responded: 2 had a complete response and 24 had a partial response. Estimated median progression-free survival was more than 7 months. None of 5 patients with melanomas lacking a BRAF mutation showed tumor regression.

Flaherty et al. (2010) reported that tumor biopsies from 7 extension-cohort patients showed markedly lower phosphorylated ERK, cyclin D1, and Ki-67 at day 15 of PLX4032 treatment than at baseline. The authors suggested that this reflected inhibition of the MAP kinase pathway. Tumor FDG uptake also fell markedly at day 15 in virtually all patients.

Flaherty et al. (2010) found that dose-limiting toxicities of PLX4032 (grade 3 rash, fatigue, and arthralgia) occurred at 1120 mg twice daily, so 960 mg twice daily became the recommended phase 2 dose. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, nearly all of the keratoacanthoma type, developed in 8 patients in the dose-escalation cohort and 10 patients in the extension cohort (31%). The median time to their appearance was 8 weeks, and none led to discontinuation of treatment.
Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin

Flaherty et al. (2010) noted that 40 to 60% of melanomas carry an activating BRAF mutation. Ninety percent of reported BRAF mutations are the V600E substitution, which constitutively activates BRAF and MAP kinase signaling.

Bollag et al. (2010) described the structure-guided discovery of PLX4032 (RG7204), a potent inhibitor of oncogenic B-RAF(V600E) kinase activity that selectively blocked the RAF/MEK/ERK pathway in BRAF-mutant cells and caused regression of BRAF-mutant xenografts. It had no effect on melanoma xenografts with wildtype BRAF. In a Phase 1 trial, 24 of 32 patients with BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma treated at the maximum tolerated dose of 960 mg twice daily had partial responses and 2 had complete responses, an 81% response rate.

Bollag et al. (2010) reported that, during dose escalation, 21 patients with metastatic melanoma (16 with and 5 without BRAF mutations) were treated at exposures with AUC greater than 300 microM-h. Ten BRAF-mutant patients had partial responses and 1 had a complete response, whereas none of the patients without BRAF mutations had a partial response. Two responders lacked the V600E mutation and instead carried BRAF V600K; they were among the better responders, with 71% and 100% reductions in tumor dimensions.

Bollag et al. (2010) found in paired tumor biopsies that more than 80% inhibition of cytoplasmic ERK phosphorylation correlated with tumor regression. Patients with plasma exposures below 300 microM-h had no measurable tumor reduction. The authors suggested that near-complete inhibition of ERK signaling may be needed for a significant tumor response.

Bollag et al. (2010) reported that 31% of patients treated at the maximum tolerated dose developed cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas of the keratoacanthoma type, usually within a few months in sun-exposed skin. These lesions were resected, and no patient discontinued treatment because of them. The authors attributed these lesions in part to paradoxical activation of the RAF/MEK/ERK pathway through RAF dimerization in cells with activated RAS.

Wei et al. (2011) performed whole-exome sequencing of 14 matched normal and metastatic tumor DNAs from untreated patients with melanoma. They identified 68 genes that appeared to be somatically mutated at elevated frequency. The mutation spectrum showed a high prevalence of C>T/G>A transitions and CC>TT/GG>AA dinucleotide substitutions, consistent with an ultraviolet light exposure signature. The BRAF V600E mutation was found in 7 of the 14 samples.

Wei et al. (2011) identified a recurrent somatic mutation in TRRAP, c.2165C>T (p.Ser722Phe), in 6 of 167 melanomas (about 4%), including the melanoma cell line A375. Sequencing all coding exons of TRRAP in 25 additional melanomas found no further nonsynonymous alterations. The affected residue is highly conserved. Because there were no truncating mutations and all alterations occurred at one position, the authors suggested that TRRAP may be a new oncogene.

Wei et al. (2011) tested the TRRAP Ser722Phe mutation functionally. Mutant TRRAP transformed NIH 3T3 cells more efficiently than wildtype TRRAP. Knocking down TRRAP with shRNA had little effect on melanoma cells with wildtype TRRAP but substantially increased apoptosis, with increased PARP cleavage, in melanoma lines carrying mutant TRRAP (63T and A375). The authors concluded that mutant TRRAP is essential for melanoma cell survival.

Wei et al. (2011) found somatic GRIN2A mutations in 6 of 14 melanomas in the exome discovery screen. In further screening they found 11 more in a prevalence screen of 38 melanomas, 11 of 39 melanomas in validation set 1, and 5 of 32 in validation set 2, plus one mutation in the 501Mel cell line. In total they identified 34 distinct GRIN2A mutations in 135 samples (25.2%). These included 2 mutation clusters (around residues 371-373 and 1073-1076), 3 recurrent alterations (S278F, E371K and E1175K), and 5 nonsense mutations. The authors said the tumorigenic mechanism was unclear, but that the mutation frequency strongly suggested a major role in melanoma.

In a pathway analysis, Wei et al. (2011) found that the glutamate signaling pathway was highly significantly mutated in melanoma. GRIN2A, which encodes an NMDA receptor subunit, and PLCB4 were frequently mutated. The authors suggested that most melanomas had alterations in genes encoding members of the glutamate signaling pathway.

Chapman et al. (2011) conducted a phase 3 randomized trial comparing the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib (960 mg orally twice daily) with dacarbazine in 675 patients with previously untreated, metastatic melanoma with the BRAF V600E mutation. At 6 months, overall survival was 84% in the vemurafenib group and 64% in the dacarbazine group. Vemurafenib was associated with a relative reduction of 63% in the risk of death and of 74% in the risk of death or disease progression (P<0.001 for both), and response rates were 48% versus 5%. After the interim analysis, crossover from dacarbazine to vemurafenib was recommended.

In the trial by Chapman et al. (2011), median progression-free survival was 5.3 months with vemurafenib and 1.6 months with dacarbazine (hazard ratio 0.26). A confirmed response occurred in 106 of 219 evaluable patients (48%) in the vemurafenib group, compared with 12 of 220 (5%) in the dacarbazine group. Among 10 vemurafenib-treated patients later found to have BRAF V600K mutations, 4 had a partial response, which the authors said indicated that melanomas with this variant are also sensitive to vemurafenib.

Chapman et al. (2011) reported that the common adverse events with vemurafenib were arthralgia, rash, fatigue, alopecia, keratoacanthoma or squamous-cell carcinoma, photosensitivity, nausea, and diarrhea. Cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma, or both developed in 61 patients (18%) and were treated by simple excision. Overall, 38% of patients needed a dose modification because of toxic effects. The authors speculated that the cutaneous neoplasia may result from vemurafenib's paradoxical activation of the MAPK pathway in cells with wild-type BRAF.

Chapman et al. (2011) stated that about 40 to 60% of cutaneous melanomas carry BRAF mutations that constitutively activate MAPK signaling. About 90% of these are V600E, and other activating mutations include V600K and V600R. In their trial, the 675 randomized patients included 20 with non-V600E mutations (19 with V600K and 1 with V600D), which were identified by Sanger and 454 sequencing.

Stark et al. (2011) performed whole-exome sequencing of 8 metastatic melanoma cell lines and matched normal lymphoblastoid cell lines and identified 3,215 somatic alterations, of which 2,139 were predicted to alter protein structure. The mutation spectrum, with a predominance of C>T/G>A transitions and CC>TT/GG>AA tandem mutations, matched the signature of ultraviolet light exposure.

Stark et al. (2011) screened 85 melanoma cell lines and found somatic nonsynonymous mutations in MAP3K5 in 8 lines (9%) and in MAP3K9 in 13 lines (15%). Taken together, 24% of samples had a mutation in one of the two genes, and with one exception the mutations were mutually exclusive. The mutations were confirmed in matched tumor DNA in all but one sample, and they did not correlate with mutations or deletions of BRAF, NRAS, CDKN2A, PTEN, or TP53.

Stark et al. (2011) found loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at MAP3K5 in 85% (98/115) of melanoma samples and at MAP3K9 in 67% (77/115). They suggested that the high LOH rate, the spread of mutations along each gene, and a MAP3K9 nonsense mutation indicated that the mutations were inactivating. They proposed that the heterozygous mutations reduce gene function through haploinsufficiency.

In in vitro kinase assays, Stark et al. (2011) found that the somatic MAP3K9 nonsense mutation W333X reduced kinase activity against myelin basic protein by 95% relative to wildtype. Expression of the mutant in HEK293T cells reduced signaling through MAP2K4/7-JNK and MEK1/2-ERK.

Stark et al. (2011) found that the somatic MAP3K5 kinase-domain mutation I780F almost abolished kinase activity (93% reduction). Structural modeling predicted that it affects helix packing in the kinase domain. In HEK293T cells, I780F reduced MAP3K5 phosphorylation and JNK signaling and decreased phospho-MEK1/2.

Stark et al. (2011) found that the somatic MAP3K5 mutation E663K, which lies next to the kinase domain and introduces a charge change, modestly but significantly reduced phosphorylation of myelin basic protein (30% reduction). In HEK293T cells it also decreased downstream phospho-MEK1/2.

Using structural modeling, Stark et al. (2011) predicted effects of three somatic MAP3K9 missense mutations found in melanoma. R160C would disrupt hydrogen bonds with E167, P263L would increase loop flexibility, and E319K would disrupt hydrogen bonding with R393.

Stark et al. (2011) found that siRNA knockdown of MAP3K9 in the melanoma cell lines UACC903 and UACC647 increased cell viability after temozolomide treatment. They suggested that reduced MAP3K9 activity can contribute to chemoresistance in melanoma.

Nikolaev et al. (2011) used exome sequencing to look for somatic mutations in protein-coding regions in 7 melanoma cell lines, comparing each with germline cells from the same donor. All melanoma samples had high numbers of somatic mutations showing the hallmark of UV-induced DNA repair. This hallmark was absent in the tumor sample-specific mutations of 2 metastases from the same individual.

Nikolaev et al. (2011) found gain-of-function somatic mutations in MAP2K1 (MEK1) and MAP2K2 (MEK2) in 2 melanomas that carried non-canonical BRAF mutations. The mutations caused constitutive ERK phosphorylation and higher resistance to MEK inhibitors. Screening a larger melanoma cohort showed recurrent somatic MAP2K1 and MAP2K2 mutations at an overall frequency of 8%.
Nikolaev et al. (2011) frequently found somatic missense and nonsense mutations in 3 candidate melanoma genes: FAT4, LRP1B, and DSC1.

Straussman et al. (2012) developed a co-culture system to test 23 stromal cell types for their effect on how 45 cancer cell lines responded to 35 anticancer drugs. They found that stroma-mediated resistance was common, especially to targeted agents. In BRAF V600E melanoma cell lines, 6 of 18 stromal (fibroblast) lines conferred resistance to the RAF inhibitor PLX4720 through secreted factors. Antibody-array analysis identified hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) as the secreted factor that best correlated with resistance.

Straussman et al. (2012) performed immunohistochemistry on pretreatment biopsies from 34 patients with BRAF V600E melanoma. HGF was detected in tumor-associated stromal cells in 23 of the 34 patients (68%). Patients with stromal HGF responded significantly worse to BRAF inhibitor treatment than patients without it (P less than 0.05). The single patient with a durable complete response lacked HGF expression.

Straussman et al. (2012) showed that recombinant HGF was both necessary and sufficient to make BRAF-mutant melanoma cells resistant to RAF inhibition. HGF was the only one of 22 receptor tyrosine kinase ligands tested that gave substantial resistance. HGF activated MET and caused sustained reactivation of both the MAPK (ERK) and PI3K/AKT pathways. The authors proposed that, during BRAF inhibition, this happened through RAF1 bypassing BRAF. Blocking HGF with a neutralizing antibody or blocking MET with crizotinib reversed the resistance, and the authors suggested combined RAF plus HGF or MET inhibition as a therapeutic strategy.

Wilson et al. (2012) tested 41 kinase-addicted human cancer cell lines against 6 receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) ligands. Nearly all lines could be rescued from kinase-inhibitor-induced growth inhibition by one or more RTK ligands. In BRAF-mutant melanoma cells, HGF was one of very few factors among 446 secreted factors tested that rescued the cells from the BRAF inhibitor PLX4032 (vemurafenib).

Wilson et al. (2012) found that HGF significantly reduced PLX4032 sensitivity in 5 of 12 additional BRAF-mutant melanoma cell lines. MET expression correlated with HGF rescue. In rescued lines, HGF reactivated MAPK signalling, and the MET inhibitor crizotinib blocked the rescue. One line (624MEL) had autocrine MET activation, and MET inhibition delayed PLX4032 resistance in this line. Crizotinib also prevented PLX4032 resistance in the A375 and 928MEL lines.

In mouse xenografts of the BRAF-mutant melanoma lines 928MEL and 624MEL, Wilson et al. (2012) found that activating MET with the agonistic antibody 3D6 strongly reduced the growth-suppressive effect of PLX4032. Inhibiting MET enhanced PLX4032-induced tumour regression.

Wilson et al. (2012) measured pretreatment plasma HGF in 126 of 132 patients with BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma treated with PLX4032 in the BRIM2 trial. Higher plasma HGF was associated with worse progression-free survival (hazard ratio 1.42, P less than 0.005) and overall survival (hazard ratio 1.8, P less than 0.001). Because the study was single-arm, the authors could not determine whether higher HGF confers drug resistance, but suggested a potential role for HGF in the response to BRAF inhibition.

Das Thakur et al. (2013) selected vemurafenib-resistant tumours by giving vemurafenib continuously to mice carrying a patient-derived xenograft of BRAF T1799A (V600E)-mutant melanoma (HMEX1906). Exome sequencing found no secondary mutations in BRAF, NRAS, KRAS, HRAS or MEK1. Instead, all 9 resistant tumours had higher levels of BRAF(V600E) mRNA and protein, and 1 tumour had BRAF amplification (about 14 copies, compared with about 6 in the parental tumour). Resistant tumours kept a dependency on BRAF(V600E)-MEK-ERK signalling.

Das Thakur et al. (2013) found that cells from vemurafenib-resistant tumours became dependent on the drug: they proliferated best at 50 nM vemurafenib. Knocking down BRAF(V600E) partially, to the level seen in parental cells, made the resistant cells sensitive again to vemurafenib and to the MEK inhibitor AZD6244. Raising BRAF(V600E) signalling in parental cells increased pERK but reduced proliferation. The authors concluded that resistance was due to elevated BRAF(V600E) expression, and that this becomes a fitness deficit when the drug is removed.

In mice, Das Thakur et al. (2013) found that stopping vemurafenib made established drug-resistant melanomas regress. Mice given vemurafenib continuously developed lethal drug-resistant disease within 100 days. None of the mice given the drug intermittently (4 weeks on, 2 weeks off) developed drug-resistant disease over 200 days, and a second patient-derived xenograft (HMEX2613) gave similar results. The authors suggested that intermittent dosing could delay the onset of drug resistance in BRAF-mutant melanoma.

Horn et al. (2013) studied a melanoma-prone family using linkage analysis and high-throughput sequencing. They found a germline mutation in the promoter of the TERT gene that segregated with disease. The mutation created a new binding motif for Ets transcription factors and ternary complex factors (TCFs) near the transcription start site. In reporter gene assays, it increased transcription up to twofold.

nodes.label: In sporadic melanoma, Horn et al. (2013) found recurrent somatic TERT promoter mutations with an ultraviolet signature. They were present in 125 of 168 (74%) cell lines derived from metastatic melanomas, 45 of 53 (85%) corresponding metastatic tumor tissues, and 25 of 77 (33%) primary melanomas. Most of these mutations occurred at 2 positions in the promoter, and they also created binding motifs for Ets/TCF transcription factors.

nodes.label: Huang et al. (2013) analyzed published whole-genome sequencing data from malignant melanomas and found two somatic TERT promoter mutations in 17 of 19 (89%) tumors. Both were C-to-T transitions at dipyrimidine motifs suggesting UV-induced damage: chr5 1,295,228 C>T (C228T) and 1,295,250 C>T (C250T). Both lay within 100 bp of the TERT transcription start site. Sanger sequencing of tumor/normal pairs confirmed the mutations, and an extension set of 51 more melanoma tumor/normal pairs found one of the two mutations in 33 tumors (65%). Altogether, 50 of 70 (71%) melanomas carried a TERT promoter mutation.

Huang et al. (2013) found that C228T and C250T never occurred together in the same melanoma (P = 5.4 x 10(-7)), which suggested the two mutations might be functionally redundant. Two tumors with C228T also had an adjacent C>T change at chr5 1,295,229, indicating a dinucleotide CC>TT transition.

Huang et al. (2013) showed that C228T and C250T each create the same 11-bp sequence, which contains a consensus binding motif for ETS transcription factors. In luciferase reporter assays in 5 cell lines, each mutation increased transcriptional activity from the TERT core promoter about 2- to 4-fold compared with the wildtype promoter.

Huang et al. (2013) proposed that the TERT promoter mutations may be driver events that act through TERT dysregulation in melanoma. Taken together, the mutations were more frequent than BRAF and NRAS mutations. Other recurrent mutations were absent from the 3 kb upstream of the TERT start site, and the mutations were absent from 24 lung adenocarcinomas with similarly high mutation rates. The authors suggested the mutations may be early events in melanoma genesis.

Huang et al. (2013) found C228T or C250T in 24 of 150 (16%) cancer cell lines from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia. These included 5 of 6 melanoma lines, 3 of 3 bladder cancer lines, and 4 of 6 hepatocellular cancer lines.

Sun et al. (2014) found that 6 of 16 melanoma tumors acquired EGFR expression after resistance to BRAF or MEK inhibitors developed. In 4 of the 6 EGFR-positive drug-resistant patient samples, they found evidence of SOX10 loss and/or activation of TGF-beta signaling.

In a chromatin-regulator-focused shRNA screen, Sun et al. (2014) found that suppressing SOX10 in melanoma activated TGF-beta signaling. This led to upregulation of EGFR and PDGFRB, which made the cells resistant to BRAF and MEK inhibitors. EGFR expression or TGF-beta treatment produced slow growth with hallmarks of oncogene-induced senescence, but helped the cells proliferate when BRAF or MEK inhibitors were present.

In mixed populations of melanoma cells, Sun et al. (2014) found that cells with low SOX10 and high EGFR expression were rapidly enriched in the presence of drug, but this enrichment reversed when the drug was stopped. They suggested that this explains why some BRAF- or MEK-inhibitor-resistant patients may regain sensitivity after a 'drug holiday', and that patients with EGFR-positive melanoma may benefit from re-treatment after one.

Van Allen et al. (2015) performed whole-exome sequencing on pretreatment tumor biopsies and matched germline samples from 110 patients with metastatic melanoma who were treated with ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4). Nonsynonymous mutational load was significantly associated with clinical benefit (P = 0.0076), and so was predicted neoantigen load (P = 0.027). Clinical variables such as age, sex, histology and LDH levels did not correlate with response.

Van Allen et al. (2015) found no gene enriched for nonsynonymous somatic mutations, including BRAF and NRAS, in either the patients who benefited from ipilimumab or those who did not. Recurrent neoantigens were rare: 28 of 77,803 unique neoantigens were found only in more than one responder. A previously reported tetrapeptide signature was not enriched among responders.

In tumor transcriptome data from 42 patients, Van Allen et al. (2015) found that expression of the cytolytic markers granzyme A (GZMA) and perforin (PRF1) was significantly higher in patients who benefited from ipilimumab (P = 0.042). Expression of CTLA4 and PD-L2 was also higher in this group (P = 0.033 and P = 0.041). The authors suggested that expression of immune checkpoint molecules may correlate with response to immunotherapy.

Hayward et al. (2017) carried out whole-genome sequencing of cutaneous, acral and mucosal melanomas. Cutaneous melanoma carried many coding and non-coding mutations, with new mutation signatures that the authors attributed to ultraviolet radiation. Significantly mutated genes in cutaneous melanoma included BRAF, CDKN2A, NRAS and TP53. In acral melanoma they were BRAF, NRAS and NF1, and in mucosal melanoma SF3B1.

Hayward et al. (2017) found that acral and mucosal melanomas were dominated by structural changes and by mutation signatures of unknown cause that had not been seen in melanoma before. The authors concluded that melanoma subtypes involve diverse carcinogenic processes, some unrelated to sun exposure.

Hayward et al. (2017) found that TERT promoter mutations were the most frequent somatic mutations in melanoma. However, neither TERT promoter mutations nor ATRX mutations were associated with greater telomere length. Recurrent non-coding mutations affected about as many genes as recurrent coding mutations.
Hayward et al. (2017) reported that most melanomas had potentially actionable mutations. Most of these were in components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase and phosphoinositol kinase pathways.
